meta.titre: Food Chains: Trophic Levels, Energy Transfer and Pyramids
meta.sous_theme: Trophic levels, energy flow and ecological pyramids

sections.contenu_markdown: A farmer in the Mbam valley grows maize and keeps goats and chickens. When she sells maize at the market she feeds many families, but when she sells a goat she feeds only a few. The reason is how energy passes along a food chain: a little is stored at each step and most is lost. This idea explains why predators are fewer than prey and why crops can feed more people than meat. Your exam will test trophic levels, pyramid shapes and energy transfer calculations.

items: Green plants make food by photosynthesis, using light energy.
Herbivores eat plants and carnivores eat animals.
Respiration releases energy and heat from food.
A percentage is part divided by whole times 100.

sections.titre: Trophic levels, energy transfer and ecological pyramids
sections.contenu_markdown:
A **food chain** shows the feeding relationships and the direction of energy flow between organisms. Each step is a **trophic level**. The arrows point from the organism that is eaten to the organism that eats it, because they show the direction in which energy and biomass move.

| Trophic level | Name | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Producer | Grass, maize, phytoplankton |
| 2 | Primary consumer (herbivore) | Goat, grasshopper |
| 3 | Secondary consumer (carnivore) | Lizard, wildcat |
| 4 | Tertiary consumer | Hawk, python |

**Decomposers** (bacteria and fungi) and detritivores feed on dead material at every level and return nutrients to the soil. A **food web** is a set of linked food chains. Many animals, including humans, are **omnivores** and feed at more than one trophic level.

**Energy flow.** Producers capture only a small part of the light that reaches them. At each transfer only about **10%** (in practice $5$ to $20\%$) of the energy passes to the next level. The rest is lost as heat from respiration, as parts not eaten (bones, roots), as undigested material in faeces and in excretory products. Energy is not destroyed; it is transferred to the environment as heat, so energy **flows one way**, whereas nutrients are **recycled**.

$$\text{efficiency of transfer}=\frac{\text{energy in the higher trophic level}}{\text{energy in the lower trophic level}}\times100$$

**Pyramids.** A pyramid of **numbers** shows the number of organisms at each level, a pyramid of **biomass** shows the dry mass of living material at each level, and a pyramid of **energy** shows the energy transferred per unit area per year. Because energy is lost at each step, there are few trophic levels, usually four or five, and a pyramid of energy is **always upright**.

variantes.nom: Inverted pyramids of numbers and biomass
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the producer is very large, when parasites are included, or when the organisms are microscopic
variantes.contenu_markdown: A pyramid of **numbers** is inverted when one large producer, such as a mango tree, supports many insects, or when many parasites live on one host. A pyramid of **biomass** can be inverted in an ocean or lake where microscopic phytoplankton have a small mass at one moment but reproduce very quickly, so the large mass of zooplankton is supported by a high rate of production. Even then the **pyramid of energy remains upright**, because it measures energy over a whole year.

variantes.nom: Efficiency and the food supply for people
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked which food gives the most energy to a large human population
variantes.contenu_markdown: The fewer the energy transfers, the more energy reaches the final consumer. People who eat grain, tubers or vegetables feed at trophic level $2$ and receive a larger share of the energy captured by the crop than people who eat meat from animals fed on the same crop, which feed at level $3$. This is why rice, wheat and cassava, grown directly for human food, support more people per hectare than cattle.

sections.enonce_markdown: In a savanna food chain, grass fixes $12\,000\ \mathrm{kJ\,m^{-2}\,year^{-1}}$. Grasshoppers receive $1\,200$, lizards receive $180$ and hawks receive $18$ of the same units. Calculate the efficiency of each transfer, the energy lost between grass and grasshoppers, and the percentage of the grass's energy that reaches the hawks.

etapes.action: Write the chain and number the trophic levels.
etapes.justification: The arrows go from the food to the feeder, and each organism occupies a trophic level.
Efficiency is energy in the higher level divided by energy in the lower level, times 100.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Grass to grasshopper $\dfrac{1\,200}{12\,000}\times100=10\%$; grasshopper to lizard $\dfrac{180}{1\,200}\times100=15\%$; lizard to hawk $\dfrac{18}{180}\times100=10\%$

etapes.action: Calculate the energy lost between grass and grasshoppers.
etapes.justification: Energy lost is the energy in the lower level that does not reach the next level.

etapes.action: Calculate the overall fraction reaching the hawks.
etapes.justification: Divide the energy in the top level by the energy in the producers.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The efficiencies are **10%, 15% and 10%**, **$10\,800\ \mathrm{kJ\,m^{-2}\,year^{-1}}$** is lost at the first transfer, and only **0.15%** of the energy fixed by grass reaches the hawks, which explains why top consumers are rare.

items.erreur_markdown: In a food chain the arrow points from the predator to its prey.
items.pourquoi_faux: The arrow shows the direction of energy flow, so it points from the organism that is eaten to the organism that eats it.
items.correction_markdown: Arrows point **from food to feeder**, for example grass $\rightarrow$ goat.

items.erreur_markdown: The energy lost at each trophic level is destroyed.
items.pourquoi_faux: Energy cannot be destroyed. It is lost from the food chain as heat from respiration, and as faeces and parts that are not eaten.
items.correction_markdown: The energy is **transferred to the surroundings as heat**, which is why energy flows in one direction.

items.erreur_markdown: Exactly 10% of the energy passes to the next level every time.
items.pourquoi_faux: The 10% is an average. Real values range from about $5\%$ to $20\%$ depending on the organisms, as the worked example shows.
items.correction_markdown: Say about 10%, or typically $5$ to $20\%$, and use the data supplied in a calculation.

items.erreur_markdown: A pyramid of energy can be inverted.
items.pourquoi_faux: Energy is lost at every transfer, so a pyramid of energy, measured over a year, is always upright. Only pyramids of numbers or biomass can be inverted.

items.erreur_markdown: Humans always feed at trophic level 3.
items.pourquoi_faux: Humans are omnivores. They are primary consumers when they eat rice or cassava, and secondary consumers when they eat meat or fish.
items.correction_markdown: A human occupies **level 2 or 3** depending on the food eaten.

items.enonce_markdown:
Study the food chain: cassava leaf $\rightarrow$ caterpillar $\rightarrow$ insectivorous bird $\rightarrow$ hawk.

(a) Name the producer.
(b) Give the trophic level of the caterpillar and the hawk.
(c) Name the type of consumer that the bird is.
(d) State the effect on the bird population of a disease that kills most of the caterpillars.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Cassava** (the leaf) is the producer.

(b) The caterpillar is at **trophic level 2** and the hawk at **trophic level 4**.

(c) The bird is a **secondary consumer** (a carnivore, more exactly an insectivore).

(d) The bird population would **decrease** because of the loss of food; the hawk population would later fall as well.

items.enonce_markdown:
A field of maize contains $60\,000\ \mathrm{kJ}$ of energy in its grain. A person needs $10\,000\ \mathrm{kJ}$ of food energy per day. Assume that people eat all of any food they are given.

(a) For how many person-days does the maize feed people if it is eaten directly?
(b) Instead the maize is fed to chickens, which convert $10\%$ of the energy in the grain to tissue that people then eat. For how many person-days does this feed people?
(c) A farmer feeds $60\,000\ \mathrm{kJ}$ of maize to chickens and they gain $4\,800\ \mathrm{kJ}$ of tissue. Calculate the percentage efficiency of the transfer.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\dfrac{60\,000}{10\,000}=$ **6 person-days**.

(b) Energy in chickens $=0.10\times60\,000=6\,000\ \mathrm{kJ}$, so $\dfrac{6\,000}{10\,000}=$ **0.6 person-days**, ten times less than eating maize directly.

(c) Efficiency $=\dfrac{4\,800}{60\,000}\times100=$ **8%**, which lies in the normal range of $5$ to $20\%$.

items.enonce_markdown:
In a lake the standing crop of phytoplankton is $4\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-2}}$ dry mass, while the standing crop of the zooplankton that eat them is $10\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-2}}$. The phytoplankton produce $400\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-2}}$ dry mass per year.

(a) State the shape of the pyramid of biomass and explain how it is possible.
(b) Calculate how many times the phytoplankton biomass is replaced per year, and the average time in days for one replacement.
(c) State the shape of the pyramid of energy for this lake and explain why.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The pyramid of biomass is **inverted**, because the zooplankton biomass ($10\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-2}}$) is greater than that of the producers ($4\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-2}}$). It is possible because the phytoplankton are eaten and replaced very quickly, so a small standing crop supports a larger biomass of consumers.

(b) Replacement $=\dfrac{400}{4}=$ **100 times per year**, so the average time is $\dfrac{365}{100}=$ **3.65 days**.

(c) The pyramid of energy is **upright**: the energy fixed per year by the phytoplankton is greater than that passed to the zooplankton, because energy is lost at each transfer.

items_markdown: A food chain shows feeding relationships; **arrows point from food to feeder** and show the direction of energy flow.
Trophic levels are producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer and so on; decomposers feed on dead material at all levels.
Only about **10%** ($5$ to $20\%$) of energy passes to the next level; the rest is lost as heat, faeces, excretion and uneaten parts.
Efficiency = energy in the higher level divided by energy in the lower level, times 100.
Pyramids of numbers and biomass can be inverted; **pyramids of energy never are**.
Eating at a lower trophic level (grain instead of meat) gives more energy per hectare to a human population.
